articles.title: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away
articles.summary: Women in the team, which is recognised by Fifa, say football has given them freedom and independence.
articles.content:
The changing room is busy with footballers going through their pre-match routines. Some stretch and tighten their boots, others embrace.

"Be strong as always because we are representing Afghan women," says midfielder Fatima Haidari to fellow members of Afghan Women United.

Applause erupts in the room where an Afghan flag hangs and a patriotic song is played. As the women sing along some struggle to hold back tears.

There's a final team huddle with words of encouragement from their coach before they head out to the pitch – a place that for years they had been told they did not belong.

The 23-player squad, selected from Afghan players now living abroad, has travelled to New Zealand for a training camp and to play two unofficial friendly games against the Cook Islands.

This is the first time they have been together since football governing body Fifa ruled in April that they could represent their country in official matches in the future.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights Afghan women footballers overcoming bans at home to reunite and represent their country internationally, symbolizing progress in women's freedom and independence. This has broad societal significance for gender equality and empowerment, with clear context and emotional impact.
articles.personality_title: Afghan women’s football team reunites abroad after home ban
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Afghanistan, women have faced bans on playing football, stopping them from competing or training freely in their own country.

**What happened** – A group of 23 Afghan women football players, now living abroad, gathered in New Zealand for a training camp. They also played two friendly matches against the Cook Islands. This is the first time they have been together since FIFA, the global football organization, allowed them to officially represent Afghanistan in future matches.

**Impact** – This reunion shows how football gives these women a chance to express themselves and feel independent, despite the restrictions they faced back home. It also sends a message about women’s rights and the possibility of change in Afghanistan.

**What’s next step** – The team will continue training and hope to participate in official international games, representing Afghanistan on the world stage.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Afghan women footballers banned at home have reunited abroad, marking a new chapter for their sport and freedom.

articles.title: Indigenous stories are global stories
articles.summary: “Even after the fall of empires and political decolonization, we, Indigenous peoples, continue to struggle for recognition and to protect and advance our fundamental rights in the world.”
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples, to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, and community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Wherever you live on this planet, there is a strong possibility that your city, town or village is built on Indigenous lands. The Canadian non-profit Native Land Digital created an interactive atlas that shows where Indigenous societies have existed for centuries in the Americas and Oceania, as well as in northern and western Africa, northern Europe, Siberia, and East Asia. This mapping exercise of historical and contemporary Indigenous territories is still, however, incomplete. It is not just that it does not show all Indigenous presence in Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The exercise would still be incomplete without integrating the fundamentally global importance of Indigenous histories and perspectives, which this GV thematic programming seeks to do this month.

I am a Maya researcher from the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico (which means that I am an Indigenous person), and I currently live, work, and learn in W8banakiak wdakiw8k, the traditional unceded territory of the Abenaki people, in what is today southern Quebec, Canada. This land acknowledgement aims to be more than a conventional gesture and, rather, to be a show of respect and gratitude to the people who have welcomed and shared their cultural and historical knowledge with me as an Indigenous guest in their home.

We, Indigenous peoples, are persons and societies that descend from those who lived in a particular territory before its colonization and settlement by other peoples, or before the creation of modern nation states which incorporated said territory. Although the term “Indigenous” etymologically means “born from the place,” it has been exclusively applied in history to societies framed by Western powers and national governments as “natural,” “rustic,” “savage,” “primitive,” or “uncivilized.” This makes ours a particular type of stateless society within modern nation-states — type of racialized society often considered too “different,” “rudimentary,” and “unmanageable” to be accepted as a self-determined nation within current state structures.

We have often been identified or called Indios or “Indians,” “Aboriginals,” “Natives,” “Bushmen,” “Berbers,” or “Tribals.” However, we have more recently demanded to be called by the names we choose, usually reclaiming our own historical names, for example, Original Peoples, First Nations, Adivasi, Maya, Inuit, Sami, Ainu, Māori, Khoisan, Amazigh, among others.

Our Indigenous languages, identities, forms of knowledge and ways of life have been maintained and transformed for hundreds of years despite territorial dispossession, forced assimilation, political and economic exclusion and, in quite a few cases, cultural genocide. Even after the fall of empires and political decolonization, we, Indigenous peoples, continue to struggle for recognition and to protect and advance our fundamental rights in the world. These rights hinge on territorial access and political self-governance, and on maintaining our livelihoods and our relationship with the land, both within and across national borders.

Contrary to conventional thought, rather than presenting Indigenous stories as past or marginal stories, I want to highlight their importance as global stories. Their significance stems from the fact that while Indigenous peoples represent approximately 6.2 percent of the global population, the territories we continue to occupy, maintain and steward amount to 25 percent of the planet’s landmass, and house a significant portion of earth's biodiversity. The importance of this biodiversity for the future survival of our species cannot be underestimated. A key fact in this story is that while the “primitivism” or “lack of technology” attributed to Indigenous peoples has often been argued as an explanation for this conservation of natural diversity, recent studies demonstrate that it is, in fact, the multifaceted and intricate Indigenous landscape management which has originated, cared for, and expanded such diversity. It has thus become crucial to heed the knowledge, cultural practices and experiences of these diverse peoples in whose hands this crucial resource has not only been preserved but keeps thriving. This commitment to the protection of the land and all the life that inhabits it (which we consider our other-than-human relatives: animals, plants, mountains, waters) frequently puts lives in danger, with reports showing that environmental activists kidnapped and murdered are disproportionately Indigenous earth defenders.

Today we are around 476 million people in the world who identify or are identified as belonging to an Indigenous people, nation and/or community. Our societies have in many cases inhabited and thrived in the same lands for hundreds, if not thousands, of years. We have often found ourselves living outside of (and resisting the pressure to be fully assimilated by) mainstream national cultures, yet we have also contributed to global cultural and scientific advancement. Indigenous peoples have added maize, tea, potato, peanut, maple syrup, chilli, quinoa, avocado, cacao, stevia, aspirin, quinine, and other products, to the diets and the pharmacies of the world, as well as to the development of canoeing, kayaking, lacrosse, hockey, the Enlightenment, constitutional federalism, legal pluralism, multi-crop agriculture, land management, botany, among other fields of human endeavour.

Indigenous worlds are as diverse as our languages, which represent the majority of the 7,000 still spoken in the world. They are, however, threatened by racial and political discrimination, and by economic marginalization. Through Rising Voices, a Global Voices program, we support communities of Indigenous activists in their efforts to reclaim, maintain and increase visibility for their languages.

We, Indigenous peoples, inhabit the Arctic regions, the plains, the pine and the rain forests, the deserts, the savannas, the mountains, the coasts, the islands, as well as some of the largest cities in the world. Mexico City, Guatemala City, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Toronto, Barcelona, Sydney, Los Angeles, Auckland, Rio de Janeiro, Hokkaido, and Lima, among others, are home to thousands if not millions of Indigenous people today.

Although Indigenous peoples have made significant advances to be recognized as distinct members of the global community at the beginning of this century — with the adoption of the Declaration of Rights of Indigenous Peoples by the United Nations Assembly in 2007 — we continue to face constant pressure by national governments, multinational companies, extractive industries, and even carbon capturing schemes, wind and solar energy farms, and data centers to give up control over the use of our territories. These are still seen as “empty lands,” which is the same principle that justified colonization and genocide in a not-so-remote past.

Like those of many other excluded communities, Indigenous perspectives are fundamental to the construction of better worlds founded on diversity, relationality and reciprocity. These perspectives are, however, almost never present in mainstream media, and when they are, they tend to show a dehumanized image of Indigenous peoples plagued by either racist stereotypes or by over-simplification, romanticization, and exoticization. This is fortunately changing, and with this August’s thematic programming by Global Voices the hope is that more people will have a chance to know first-hand the Indigenous voices that are part of our global network.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the global significance of Indigenous peoples' rights, cultures, and environmental stewardship, emphasizing their ongoing struggle for recognition and protection of fundamental rights. It provides substantial context on Indigenous contributions to biodiversity, culture, and knowledge, and advocates for visibility and respect, which has broad societal and environmental impact.
articles.personality_title: Indigenous stories connect people and protect the planet
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Indigenous peoples are the original inhabitants of lands around the world. Despite centuries of colonization and challenges, they continue to protect their cultures, languages, and rights. Many cities today stand on lands that once belonged to Indigenous communities.

**What happened** – A new series by Global Voices in August 2026 highlights Indigenous rights and stories from around the world. It shares experiences of Indigenous leaders, activists, and communities to raise awareness and respect for their cultures and struggles. The series also features a map created by Native Land Digital that shows Indigenous territories across the Americas, Oceania, Africa, Europe, and Asia.

**Impact** – Indigenous peoples make up about 6.2% of the world’s population but live on 25% of the Earth’s land, including areas rich in plants and animals. Their careful management of these lands has helped preserve biodiversity for centuries. Indigenous knowledge and traditions have also contributed many foods, medicines, and cultural practices used worldwide today. Highlighting these stories challenges old stereotypes and helps people understand the important role Indigenous peoples play in protecting the environment and enriching global culture.

**What's next step** – Global Voices and other groups plan to continue sharing Indigenous voices to increase recognition and support for their rights. This includes protecting their land from industries that threaten it and helping Indigenous languages and cultures thrive. More people learning about these stories can lead to better respect and cooperation between Indigenous communities and others.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Indigenous peoples’ stories and knowledge are vital to understanding our world’s history, protecting nature, and shaping a diverse future.

articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: Tate brothers’ US extradition case a ‘step towards accountability,’ says independent expert
articles.summary: An independent UN human rights expert has welcomed ongoing proceedings in the United States to extradite “manosphere” bloggers Andrew and Tristan Tate to the United Kingdom, calling the case an important step towards accountability for serious allegations of violence against women and girls.
articles.content:
The proceedings “offer renewed hope that justice may finally be achieved through effective international cooperation,” said Reem Alsalem, Special Rapporteur on violence against women and girls.

She noted that the action taken comes after years in which women’s testimonies and experiences had been ignored or dismissed by law enforcement and prosecutorial authorities.

Tweet URL

Call for justice

“Given the scale of the alleged offences, and the Tate brothers’ global influence in promoting misogyny and harmful models of masculinity, it is urgent and imperative that they face justice,” she said.

The Tate brothers – dual British-US nationals and former professional kickboxers-turned-social media influencers – were arrested in Miami, Florida, on 18 July following an extradition request from the UK.

They remain in custody in the US while challenging the extradition request, where they face 59 criminal charges, including rape, sexual assault, facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, assault, and offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.

Separate criminal proceedings remain ongoing in Romania concerning allegations including human trafficking, including the trafficking of minors.

‘No one should be above the law’

Ms. Alsalem urged the Governments of Romania, the UK and the US to ensure that the Tate brothers face justice.

"All too often, perpetrators of violence against women exploit delays, fragmented jurisdictional responses and their wealth, power or influential public profile to evade accountability,” she said, stressing that “no one should be above the law, regardless of their status, influence or international reach.”

She also called for the justice process to be expanded to include those that aided, abetted and profited from the Tate brothers’ criminal enterprise of grooming, exploiting and abusing women and girls, rather than focusing only on individual criminal responsibility.

On 4 March, Ms. Alsalem transmitted information she had received to the Governments of Romania and the United Kingdom – with copies to the United States – regarding the poor handling of allegations of rape, strangulation, intimidation and retaliation made by a woman who alleged that she had been sexually assaulted by Andrew Tate in Romania in 2018.

Special Rapporteurs are independent experts appointed by the Human Rights Council in Geneva. They are not United Nations staff and do not receive a salary for their work.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant step towards accountability for serious allegations of violence against women and girls, highlighting international cooperation and the pursuit of justice against influential perpetrators. This has broad societal impact by addressing violence against women and promoting legal accountability.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Cambodia human rights, Hormuz invasive species risk, IOM lauds 2025 progress
articles.summary: Concluding his first official visit to Cambodia, UN independent human rights expert Tom Andrews said he was encouraged by the government’s cooperation but remained concerned about key human rights issues such as the lack of freedom of expression.
articles.content:
Although Mr. Andrews was able to meet freely with local human rights advocates and people displaced by Cambodia’s ongoing border conflict with Thailand, he said many are imprisoned for exercising their political rights, prisons remain overcrowded and some senior government officials remain involved in cyberscam operations.

“My first mission to Cambodia has left me with deep concerns: for displaced people along the border with Thailand, for those who have been trafficked, and for those who are behind bars having exercised basic freedoms,” he said.

Tweet URL

Mixed progress on human rights

Mr. Andrews was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council as the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in Cambodia.

On one hand, he acknowledged that the government has taken meaningful steps to close scam compounds, agreed to address prison overcrowding, dramatically improved economic conditions for millions and committed to many human rights treaties.

On the other, he said more than 100 people may be detained for exercising basic political freedoms, many of the country’s laws conflict with international law, opposition parties are harassed and the government has not done enough to take action against scammers.

With elections approaching in 2027 and 2028, Mr. Andrews said the government must respect the rights of political opponents.

In the country’s north and northwest, more than 20,000 Cambodians remain displaced – unable to return home because their villages are occupied by Thai soldiers amid the latest flareups on the border.

He stressed that Thailand and Cambodia must work together to ensure that all civilians can return home safely.

“They need, and deserve, to go home,” he said.

Special Rapporteurs receive their mandates from the UN Human Rights Council, which is based in Geneva. They are not UN staff and do not receive payment for their work.

UN News/Daniel Dickinson

Trapped ships in Strait of Hormuz face a different kind of attack

The UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) warned that ships stranded in the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Iran war could become an “ecological timebomb,” increasing the risk of invasive species spreading to new marine environments once shipping resumes.

The concern centers on “biofouling” – the buildup of marine organisms such as algae and small animals on ship hulls. Vessels that remain stationary for extended periods face an increased risk of biofouling.

“There is a risk of a transfer of species if ships are unable to remove fouling before moving out of an area or after a prolonged period of time in one area,” said IMO spokesperson Natasha Brown. “The IMO recommends that ship operators follow the IMO biofouling guidelines as far as possible.”

Invasive species impacts could be ‘devastating’

The IMO said biofouling has become a growing global problem due to increased shipping and trade, warning that the impacts of invasive aquatic species have been “devastating” in some regions because they are difficult to remove once established.

“Bioinvasions are actually continuing at an alarming rate and there are new areas being invaded all the time,” the agency warned.

UN migration agency: Millions reached in 2025 despite mounting pressures

The UN migration agency IOM provided humanitarian assistance to 17.8 million people in 170 countries and territories in 2025 – a year marked by conflicts, disasters, record needs and a sharp drop in aid funding, according to a report published on Wednesday.

Established in 1951, the IOM provides humanitarian aid to refugees and displaced people, helps governments create safe migration policies, and works to ensure that human mobility remains humane and orderly.

Focusing its efforts on places such as Gaza, Haiti, Myanmar, Ukraine and the Sahel, the IOM provided shelter assistance to 7.3 million people last year, delivered 4.2 million primary health consultations and supported 5.1 million people with water, sanitation and hygiene services, according to the report.

In addition to the IOM’s direct on-the-ground aid, the Organization’s data informed 21 humanitarian response plans, helping governments and aid organisations target assistance.

The report highlighted the importance of coordination and evidence-based interventions to prioritise where to deliver aid as global funding continues to decrease.

“Conflicts, disasters, disease outbreaks and displacement drove needs to unprecedented levels, even as resources contracted dramatically,” IOM Deputy Director General for Operations Ugochi Daniels said.

“Despite these challenges, IOM remained present where people needed us most.”

El experto en derechos humanos de la ONU, Tom Andrews, visitó Camboya y encontró cooperación del gobierno, aunque sigue preocupado por presos políticos y conflictos fronterizos con Tailandia. Por otra parte, la Organización Marítima Internacional advirtió que los barcos varados en el Estrecho de Ormuz podrían propagar especies invasoras debido a organismos marinos en sus cascos. La visita a Camboya mostró avances como el cierre de sitios de estafa y mejoras económicas, pero también problemas graves como acoso político y familias desplazadas cerca de la frontera con Tailandia. La advertencia ambiental es importante porque las especies invasoras pueden dañar los ecosistemas marinos cuando los barcos se mueven después de largas paradas. El trabajo de la OIM es destacado por ayudar a millones en lugares difíciles como Gaza y Ucrania, demostrando cómo la cooperación global puede apoyar a personas afectadas por conflictos y desastres.

**Próximo paso** –
Camboya debe proteger las libertades políticas y colaborar con Tailandia para que los desplazados puedan regresar a casa con seguridad. La Organización Marítima está preparando un tratado para mejorar la gestión de la limpieza de barcos y reducir riesgos de especies invasoras. La OIM continuará enfocando la ayuda en las necesidades más urgentes mientras se adapta a la reducción de fondos.

Los esfuerzos de la ONU muestran avances y desafíos continuos en derechos humanos, protección ambiental y ayuda humanitaria en todo el mundo.
